\section[iniūria, iniūriae]{iniūria, iniūriae — a wrong, an injustice, an insult}

\label{lesson:LA-C414-iniuria}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to beg to be spared, then the Latin for defence in court.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: iniūria, iniūriae}
\textbf{iniūria, iniūriae} — \textquotedblleft{}a wrong, an injustice, an insult\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Iniūriam accēpit, nōn fēcit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He suffered a wrong; he did not do one.}
\end{quote}

\emph{iniūria, iniūriae} f., \emph{in-} not + \emph{iūs}: what is against right. \emph{Iniūriā}, wrongly. English \emph{injury}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{iniūria} is built from \emph{in-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{iūs, iūris} \textquotedblleft{}right, law\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short): what goes against right. English \emph{injury} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iniūria, iniūriae}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iniūria, iniūriae}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{iniūria, iniūriae}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to beg to be spared, then the Latin for defence in court, then say \emph{iniūria, iniūriae} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does iniūria, iniūriae mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A wrong, an injustice, an insult\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[flāgitium, flāgitiī]{flāgitium, flāgitiī — a disgraceful act, a scandal}

\label{lesson:LA-C414-flagitium}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for defence in court, then the Latin for a wrong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: flāgitium, flāgitiī}
\textbf{flāgitium, flāgitiī} — \textquotedblleft{}a disgraceful act, a scandal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hoc flāgitium tacēre nōn possum.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I cannot keep quiet about this scandal.}
\end{quote}

\emph{flāgitium, flāgitiī} n., a shameful deed, and the person who does it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{flāgitium} is built on \emph{flāgitō} \textquotedblleft{}to demand loudly\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short): first a furious demand, then the shameful act that people cried out against.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for defence in court, then the Latin for a wrong, then say \emph{flāgitium, flāgitiī} again

\section[fās]{fās — divine law; what is right}

\label{lesson:LA-C414-fas}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a wrong, then the Latin for a disgraceful act.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fās}
\textbf{fās} — \textquotedblleft{}divine law; what is right\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fās nōn est hoc dīcere.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is not right to say this.}
\end{quote}

\emph{fās} n., indeclinable. \emph{Fās est}, it is right, it is allowed by the gods; it covers what human law leaves out.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fās} is inherited from a Proto-Indo-European noun meaning \textquotedblleft{}a saying, an utterance\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), and Lewis \& Short link it with \emph{fārī} \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}: what the gods have declared.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fās}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fās}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{fās}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a wrong, then the Latin for a disgraceful act, then say \emph{fās} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does fās mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Divine law; what is right\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[nefās]{nefās — a crime against heaven, a wicked thing}

\label{lesson:LA-C414-nefas}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a disgraceful act, then the Latin for divine law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: nefās}
\textbf{nefās} — \textquotedblleft{}a crime against heaven, a wicked thing\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nefās est hospitem violāre.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is wicked to wrong a guest.}
\end{quote}

\emph{nefās} n., indeclinable: \emph{ne-} not + \emph{fās}. English \emph{nefarious} comes from its family.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nefās} is built from \emph{ne-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{fās} \textquotedblleft{}divine law\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short): what heaven forbids. English \emph{nefarious} comes from its adjective.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a disgraceful act, then the Latin for divine law, then say \emph{nefās} again

\section[inīquus, inīqua, inīquum]{inīquus, inīqua, inīquum — unfair, unjust; uneven}

\label{lesson:LA-C414-iniquus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for divine law, then the Latin for a crime against heaven.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: inīquus, inīqua, inīquum}
\textbf{inīquus, inīqua, inīquum} — \textquotedblleft{}unfair, unjust; uneven\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Lēx inīqua est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The law is unfair.}
\end{quote}

\emph{inīquus, inīqua, inīquum}, \emph{in-} not + \emph{aequus}, level, fair. English \emph{iniquity}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{inīquus} is built from \emph{in-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{aequus} \textquotedblleft{}level, fair\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), the vowel changed inside the compound. English \emph{iniquity} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
